name: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)
short: High doses can cause sensory neuropathy: all 5 volunteers on 1 or 3 g/day had symptoms; a review discourages >50 mg/day long term. 1982 review: B6 can lower levodopa effect (no carbidopa in abstract).
text: A 2023 systematic review of 20 articles concluded that current evidence supports a neurotoxic role of vitamin B6 at high levels: higher B6 levels, usually from supplements, may lead to a predominantly sensory neuropathy of the axonal type, and such patients reported improvement after pyridoxine was stopped; the same review found that supplementation at permitted daily doses had not been proven harmful in people who already had peripheral neuropathy. In a prospective study, five healthy volunteers given 1 or 3 g of pyridoxine a day all developed sensory symptoms with abnormal sensory-threshold tests (pyridoxine was stopped at the first abnormality), those on the higher dose earlier, and symptoms kept progressing for 2 to 3 weeks after stopping. A 2014 review concluded that pyridoxine at doses greater than 50 mg a day for extended periods may be harmful and should be discouraged, noting that before it no systematic review supported either that caution or routine supplementation. For interactions, a 1982 review of drug and vitamin B6 interactions gives a decrease by pyridoxine in the efficacy of levodopa used in Parkinsonism as an example of supplementation adversely affecting a medicine; the abstract does not say whether this applies when levodopa is combined with carbidopa.
